That IS probably the biggest problem, the 70's, 80's and even a bit of the 90's were a time of experimenting, trying things out and newness. Now? Now hollywood has become like old people. Want to just rehash the same shit over and over again and not take any chances. I do think CGI also helped in making movies even more lazy now. Nobody goes to new locations now, or create new interesting props, it is all done in green rooms with foam props. Star Wars, then and now sums it up.

To me cool SciFi is something that could be true in the future. A lot of the cool sci-fi of the past has or is becoming a reality. It may just be that were in a transition period where writers/film makers are trying to find ideas that could be true in 50 years and are missing the mark.

Also, the downfall of the B movie has led to a lack of directors coming up in the ranks who know how to do sci-fi and have the vision for it, and are willing to experiment. People forget that James Cameron was a B movie director. Terminator was a B movie. You could have B movies that opened up briefly in the summer and still made money to cover their losses - not anymore.

The studios have changed. The balance between art and money has shifted in favor of the money. Their are tons of amazing SciFi movies that probably are never made because the studios decided not to fund it.

Golden Age thinking. Read that. Try to understand it.

Yes, I know it's easy to think that things used to be so much better, whether we're talking about sci-fi or chivalry or respect for elders or whatever. You're simply just applying it to one particular thing here.

Christopher Nolan still uses practical effects. The manipulated gravity in the hotel corridor and room in Inception (I don't know whether that counts as sci fi or not) were giant dynamic sets, and TARS in Interstellar was a puppet (with CGI for the more complex movements).

A ton of cool Sci-Fi is still coming out in the 2000's! We had Serenity (2005), Donnie Darko (2001), Avatar (2009)(subjective), WALL-E (2008), The Matrix: Reloaded (2003) & Revolutions (2003), Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy (2005), The Island (2005), Watchman (2009), The Book of Eli (2010), Inception (2010), Looper (2012), Chronicle (2012)(personal favorite), The Adjustment Bureau (2011), The Last Airbender (2010), and Pacific Rim (2013). Didn't count any superhero movie or movie remakes.
Or interstellar, or the Martian or any lots of great scifi that is out there.
Also Primer and the Planet of the Apes movie series. If OP counts TV shows Black Mirror from the UK is great and Rick and Morty is awesome crazy sci-fi goodness.

Across the board films are only given large budgets if they will be accessible and successful internationally, and this doesn't just mean anglo-euro international translations like back in the 80s and 90s, but perform well in China and everything inbetween.

Without a nuanced deep shared culture movies have a few universals that translate everywhere, explosions, violence, love, explosions so they are painting with a very limited palette. Blade Runner would be a mess without sharing the cultural background.

I'd have to say it's probably a budget issue. Studios get millions upon millions of dollars to churn out the same formulaic shit because they know it makes money and it will have no problem making money. The 70's, 80's, and 90's were probably a cheaper time with less focus on the formula/money and more focus on the quality. I could be completely wrong though because I know for sure there's no loss in creative spark. If Kevin Smith and Patton Oswalt teamed up to make a Sci-Fi movie with the budget of a blockbuster, it'd probably be an instant classic.
An entire generation lost their creative spark. Everyone is plugged in. The well is poisoned.

I agree with what many here are saying with respect to Hollywood/movie studio playing it safe, but you have to realize the huge investment in money and time that they studios have to lay out for a movie. The studios are going to try to make any of their projects reach the largest group they possibly can to better their chances at recouping their investment and making a profit. This is why most of the good sci-fi movies are independent or "low" budget movies.

The real location of "good" sci-fi is television and online. For television the cost of creating the content is far lower than a movie, and even more so for online content. In my mind that is where all the cool sci-fi will be found going forward.
